title: Figgie International, Inc. v. Destileria Serralles, Inc.
summary: Uncontradicted evidence of industry practice supplied an exclusive repair, replacement, or refund remedy; the completed refund prevented that remedy from failing merely because earlier repair efforts had been unsuccessful.
notes: The printed standard-terms language is awkward. The court’s analysis consistently identifies the operative alternatives as repair, replacement, or return with repayment. The notes separately question broad exclusions of incidental and consequential damages and the distinction between commercial and consumer losses; they do not establish that every disclaimer is enforceable.

sections.Parties: Figgie manufactured bottle-labeling equipment. Destileria Serralles operated a rum-bottling plant in Puerto Rico and bought the equipment. Figgie sought a declaration limiting its liability, while Serralles sought additional breach damages.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties’ June 1993 agreement called for equipment capable of placing a clear label within a raised oval on clear bottles of Cristal rum. Problems appeared when the machinery was installed in April 1994. Figgie attempted repairs over several months, without achieving satisfactory operation. By November the machinery was returned and the purchase price refunded. Serralles nevertheless sought its losses from unsuccessful operation and delay in obtaining replacement equipment.

The written-remedy issue was factually disputed. Figgie had lost the original agreement in a reorganization and relied on its customary standard terms. Serralles produced a copy referring to conditions on the reverse, but its reverse was blank. Figgie instead offered affidavits from experienced industry participants stating that sellers consistently limited remedies to repair, replacement, or return and excluded consequential damages. Serralles supplied no contrary evidence of trade practice.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment to Figgie and denied Serralles’ request for partial summary judgment. The Fourth Circuit affirmed in 1999. The casebook divides the opinion into the trade-usage discussion at pages 593–596 and the essential-purpose discussion at pages 1043–1046; these are two parts of the same appeal.
sections.Issue: Could industry practice establish the limitation despite a dispute about the written conditions, and did unsuccessful repairs cause the exclusive remedy to fail of its essential purpose under UCC § 2-719?
sections.Holding: Trade usage supplied the exclusive remedy on the uncontradicted record. The remedy did not fail of its essential purpose because it included return and refund as well as repair or replacement, and return and refund occurred.
sections.Reasoning:
The Code’s concept of the agreement includes the parties’ language and implications from commercial circumstances. A sufficiently regular trade practice, known or appropriately attributable to parties in that trade, can supplement or qualify the express terms. Because the evidence of the industry’s remedy practice was uncontradicted, the factual dispute over the missing reverse-side conditions did not preclude judgment on the independent usage ground.

The court then assessed the remedy actually incorporated. An exclusive repair-or-replacement remedy can fail when those efforts are unsuccessful. Here, however, refund after return was another agreed option. Trying repairs first did not irrevocably elect that option or abandon the refund alternative. The sequence—repair attempts, then return and repayment—was precisely the commercially sensible progression the limitation contemplated for sophisticated equipment. The court found no evidence that the refund option itself failed.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Figgie connects interpretation and remedies: first identify the remedy the parties’ agreement contains, including trade usage, and only then decide whether that remedy remains enforceable. It demonstrates why a case needs to appear in more than one topic index.

topics.assent: Commercial context can supply a term even when evidence about the written terms is disputed.
topics.interpretation: Uses uncontradicted trade practice to supplement the agreement.
topics.trade-usage: Explains the evidentiary role of regular industry remedy practices.
topics.remedies: Applies the essential-purpose limitation to the full set of agreed alternatives.
topics.ucc: Combines the Code’s agreement definition and trade usage with § 2-719.

mnemonic.rationale: Bottling machinery that did not work
